content: 1. The study titled Estimating the non-monetary burden of neurocysticercosis in Mexico published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2012 (volume 6, article e1521) evaluates the non-financial impacts of neurocysticercosis on affected populations in Mexico. 2. Bhattarai et al. (2019) investigated the monetary burden of cysticercosis in Mexico, highlighting the economic costs associated with this parasitic disease. Their findings were published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases (volume 13, article e0007501). 3. Carabin et al. (2006) estimated the cost of Taenia solium cysticercosis in the Eastern Cape Province of South Africa. Their research, published in Tropical Medicine and International Health (volume 11, pages 906–916), provides insights into the financial implications of this disease in the region. 4. Ito et al. (2003) discussed the challenges of controlling echinococcosis and cysticercosis in China, emphasizing the need for international cooperation. This work was published in Acta Tropica (volume 86, pages 3–17). 5. Rajkotia et al. (2007) presented findings on the economic burden of neurocysticercosis in Peru, as part of the Cysticercosis Working Group of Peru. Their study appeared in Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene (volume 101, pages 840–846). 6. Zoli et al. (2003) reviewed the regional status, epidemiology, and impact of Taenia solium cysticercosis in Western and Central Africa. Their findings were published in Acta Tropica (volume 87, pages 35–42). 7. Trevisan et al. (2016) reported on severe seizures observed in pigs naturally infected with Taenia solium in Tanzania. This study was published in Veterinary Parasitology (volume 220, pages 67–71). 8. Willingham et al. (2010) explored strategies to combat Taenia solium cysticercosis in Southeast Asia, emphasizing the potential to improve human health and livestock production. Their work was published in Advances in Parasitology (volume 72, pages 235–266). 9. The World Health Organization (2020) provided an overview of the endemicity of Taenia solium through its Global Health Observatory platform, offering critical data for public health interventions. 10. The WHO's 2009 expert consultation report on foodborne trematode infections and taeniasis/cysticercosis, held in Vientiane, Lao PDR, outlined strategies for controlling these diseases. This report was published in 2011. 11. The Pan American Health Organization (2019) released operational guidelines for controlling taeniasis and cysticercosis caused by Taenia solium, emphasizing practical approaches for implementation. 12. The WHO, FAO, and OIE (2019) jointly published a guide advocating for a multisectoral, One Health approach to address zoonotic diseases, highlighting the importance of collaboration across sectors. 13. Gabrielli et al. (2011) discussed the theoretical and operational aspects of preventive chemotherapy in human helminthiasis, focusing on its application in control programs. This study appeared in Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene (volume 105, pages 683–693). 14. Haby et al. (2020) conducted a systematic review on the effectiveness of selected drugs for preventive chemotherapy against Taenia solium taeniasis. Their findings were published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases (volume 14, article e0007873). 15. The WHO's 2019 Model List of Essential Medicines includes drugs for parasitic diseases, underscoring their importance in global health initiatives. 16. The WHO's 1995 prescribing information for drugs used in parasitic diseases remains a critical resource for healthcare professionals managing these infections. 17. The WHO's 2006 manual on preventive chemotherapy in human helminthiasis provides guidance for health professionals and program managers on the coordinated use of anthelmintic drugs. 18. The WHO's 2017 guideline on preventive chemotherapy for soil-transmitted helminth infections targets at-risk population groups, offering evidence-based recommendations for control. 19. The WHO/FAO/OIE guidelines (2005) for the surveillance, prevention, and control of taeniasis/cysticercosis provide a comprehensive framework for addressing these diseases. 20. The forthcoming WHO guidelines on the management of Taenia solium neurocysticercosis aim to standardize care and improve outcomes for affected individuals. 21. The Pan American Health Organization's 2016 Plan of Action for the Elimination of Neglected Infectious Diseases outlines strategies for achieving sustainable development goals in the Americas. 22. The PAHO's 2019 Disease Elimination Initiative emphasizes an integrated, sustainable approach to communicable diseases in the Americas. 23. The WHO's 2020 roadmap for neglected tropical diseases outlines strategies to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals by 2030, focusing on ending neglect and improving health outcomes. 24. The WHO's 2014 Handbook for Guideline Development provides a systematic approach to creating evidence-based health guidelines. 25. The Oxford 2011 Levels of Evidence framework offers a standardized method for evaluating the quality of evidence in medical research. 26. Briss et al. (2000) described methods for developing evidence-based community preventive services, as outlined by the Task Force on Community Preventive Services. 27. Haby et al. (2018) reviewed the effectiveness of mass drug administration for controlling Taenia solium taeniasis in endemic areas, providing valuable insights for public health programs. 28. Hobbs et al. (2020) examined community perceptions and acceptance of Taenia solium control interventions in Zambia, highlighting the importance of community engagement in public health efforts. 29. Ramandrasoa et al. (2020) evaluated the impact of a three-year mass drug administration pilot project for taeniasis control in Madagascar, demonstrating its effectiveness in reducing disease prevalence. 30. Balshem et al. (2011) introduced the GRADE guidelines for rating the quality of evidence, providing a framework for making healthcare decisions. 31. Alonso-Coello et al. (2016) presented the GRADE Evidence to Decision frameworks, offering a transparent approach to healthcare decision-making. 32. Guyatt et al. (2008) discussed the emerging consensus on the GRADE system for rating evidence quality and recommendation strength. 33. The WHO's 2011 guide for helminth control in school-age children provides practical advice for managing control programs in this vulnerable population. 34. Yoshino (1934) described the subjective symptoms caused by Taenia solium parasitism in humans, contributing to the understanding of this disease's clinical manifestations. 35. Ito et al. (2020) revisited Yoshino's experimental infections with Taenia solium, emphasizing the ethical considerations of such studies. 36. The WHO's 2019 Bench Aids for the Diagnosis of Intestinal Parasites serves as a practical tool for laboratory professionals diagnosing parasitic infections. 37. Allan et al. (1990) developed an immunodiagnostic method for detecting taeniasis using coproantigen detection, advancing diagnostic capabilities for this disease. 38. Gueza et al. (2009) created a species-specific coproantigen ELISA for diagnosing human Taenia solium taeniasis, improving diagnostic accuracy. 39. Lightowlers et al. (2016) discussed monitoring outcomes of interventions against Taenia solium, providing suggestions for evaluating program effectiveness. 40. O'Neal et al. (2014) explored the use of ring-screening to control endemic transmission of Taenia solium, demonstrating its potential as a public health strategy. 41. Bustos et al. (2012) identified coproantigen detection as an early indicator of treatment failure for taeniasis, emphasizing its role in monitoring therapeutic outcomes. 42. Varma et al. (1990) compared the efficacy of mebendazole, flubendazole, and niclosamide against human tapeworm infections, providing evidence for treatment selection. 43. Allan et al. (1997) evaluated the impact of mass chemotherapy on the prevalence of Taenia solium infections in humans and pigs, demonstrating its effectiveness as a control measure. 44. Garcia et al. (2016) reported on the elimination of Taenia solium transmission in northern Peru, highlighting the success of integrated control strategies. 45. Gamboa et al. (2017) assessed the efficacy and adverse events of niclosamide in a large-scale cysticercosis elimination program in Peru, providing evidence for its use in public health initiatives. 46. Groll (1980) reviewed the use of praziquantel for treating cestode infections in humans, establishing its efficacy and safety profile. 47. Kumar et al. (2014) studied the prevalence of intestinal worm infestations and the efficacy of anthelmintic drugs, contributing to the understanding of treatment outcomes. 48. Moreira et al. (1983) evaluated the treatment of human taeniasis caused by Taenia saginata or Taenia solium with praziquantel, confirming its effectiveness. 49. Rim et al. (1979) investigated the therapeutic effects of praziquantel against Taenia solium infections, providing evidence for its clinical use. 50. Taylor et al. (1995) examined targeted chemotherapy for parasite infestations in rural preschool children, demonstrating its impact on reducing disease burden. 51. Cruz et al. (1989) conducted operational studies on controlling Taenia solium taeniasis/cysticercosis in Ecuador, providing insights into effective intervention strategies. 52. Sarti et al. (2000) evaluated mass treatment against human taeniasis for controlling cysticercosis, demonstrating its population-level impact. 53. Steinmann et al. (2011) conducted a randomized controlled trial on the control of soil-transmitted helminthiasis, providing evidence for intervention effectiveness. 54. Steinmann et al. (2008) conducted an open-label randomized trial on soil-transmitted helminthiasis, contributing to the understanding of treatment outcomes. 55. Jagota (1986) studied the use of albendazole for treating intestinal nematode and cestode infections, confirming its broad-spectrum efficacy. 56. De Kaminsky (1991) evaluated albendazole treatment in human taeniasis, providing evidence for its clinical application. 57. Steinmann et al. (2015) reviewed experiences and lessons from a five-year multi-intervention trial for controlling soil-transmitted helminthiasis in Yunnan Province, China. 58. Flisser et al. (1993) reported on neurological symptoms in occult neurocysticercosis following a single taeniacidal dose of praziquantel, highlighting potential adverse effects. 59. Pearson and Hewlett (1985) reviewed niclosamide therapy for tapeworm infections, establishing its efficacy and safety. 60. The WHO's PCT databank provides critical data for managing neglected tropical diseases through preventive chemotherapy. 61. The WHO's Weekly Epidemiological Record serves as a key resource for tracking global health trends and interventions. 62. Wandra et al. (2016) presented a case study of neurocysticercosis diagnosed after praziquantel administration in a patient with Taenia saginata taeniasis, emphasizing the importance of accurate diagnosis. 63. Ramos-Zuniga et al. (2013) discussed the incidental consequences of anthelmintic treatment in the central nervous system, highlighting potential risks. 64. Garcia et al. (2007) reported on neurocysticercosis uncovered by single-dose albendazole, emphasizing the need for careful monitoring during treatment. 65. Lillie and McGann (2010) cautioned against empirical albendazole therapy in patients with new-onset seizures, highlighting potential risks. 66. O'Neal et al. (2012) reported on neurocysticercosis among resettled refugees from Burma, emphasizing the importance of screening in high-risk populations. 67. Bardosh et al. (2014) explored the biosocial complexity of One Health interventions for neglected zoonotic helminths in northern Lao PDR, emphasizing the need for integrated approaches. 68. Keilbach et al. (1989) described a program to control taeniasis-cysticercosis in a Mexican village, providing insights into community-based interventions. 69. Okello et al. (2016) assessed the impact of a joint human-porcine intervention package for Taenia solium control in northern Lao PDR, demonstrating its effectiveness. 70. Olds et al. (1999) conducted a double-blind placebo-controlled study on the concurrent administration of albendazole and praziquantel in schoolchildren with schistosomiasis and geohelminths, providing evidence for combination therapy. 71. Yajima et al. (2011) identified moderate and high endemicity of schistosomiasis as predictors of soil-transmitted helminthiasis endemicity, emphasizing the need for integrated control strategies. 72. Jung et al. (1997) studied the clinical pharmacokinetics of albendazole in children with neurocysticercosis, providing insights into its use in pediatric populations. 73. Jung et al. (1997) also investigated the pharmacokinetics of albendazole in patients with brain cysticercosis, contributing to the understanding of its therapeutic profile.
